lessons.title: How algorithms shape your 'for you' feed

steps.title: What's an algorithm again?
steps.body: TikTok, Instagram, and YouTube don't just show you everything — an algorithm selects what you see, based on what you clicked, liked, or watched for a long time before. These days, news often reaches you through a feed like this, rather than a newspaper or news site you look up yourself.

steps.title: The filter bubble
steps.body: Because the algorithm mostly shows you things that match what you already like, you can end up in a filter bubble: seeing more and more of the same kind of opinions, and less and less of the opposite view — without even noticing.

steps.title: Deliberately stepping outside the bubble
steps.body: Deliberately follow a few accounts with a different angle than you're used to, and occasionally use targeted search instead of just scrolling your 'for you' feed.

steps.title: Exercise
steps.body: Think about it: which three sources do you see most often on TikTok or Instagram? Are those different angles, or mostly the same voice?

steps.title: Fake photos and videos
steps.body: AI can create convincing fake photos and videos of events that never happened, or of well-known faces saying things they never said. Watch for unnatural details — odd hands, shadows that don't line up right, unnaturally smooth 'plastic' skin.

steps.title: Spotting AI-written articles and 'fake influencers'
steps.body: Some fake news sites use AI to generate articles in bulk, and fully AI-generated 'influencers' now exist and run ads. Watch for: very generic language, no clear author, and content that's mostly rewritten snippets from other sites.

steps.title: Reverse image search
steps.body: Not sure about a photo or screenshot going around in a group chat? Use Google Lens or a reverse image search to check whether the photo already appeared online before, in a different context.

steps.title: Exercise
steps.body: Browse a recent photo below and try to trace its source using a search engine.

steps.title: Using fact-check sites
steps.body: Sites like Nieuwscheckers or international fact-checkers investigate widely shared claims (viral TikTok and Instagram claims included) and explain what's true and what isn't.

steps.title: Lateral reading
steps.body: Instead of only judging the post or site itself, open a new tab and search for what others say about that source or message. This quickly gives you a sense of its reliability.

steps.title: Comparing multiple sources
steps.body: Look for the same news at at least two independent, well-known sources. Do they tell the same story, with the same facts? Then it's more likely to be true.

steps.title: Exercise
steps.body: Pick a news story or viral moment you saw recently on social media, and look it up at at least two other sources.

steps.title: Why sharing quickly can be harmful
steps.body: Research shows fake news often spreads faster than the correction that follows it — especially on platforms that reward speed and engagement. Once shared, a false message is hard to undo, even if you delete it later.

steps.title: Check before you share (or repost)
steps.body: A few extra seconds of checking before clicking 'Share' or 'Repost' prevents you from contributing to the spread of something false.

steps.title: Correcting someone kindly
steps.body: Noticed someone in your group chat sharing fake news? Reply kindly with a reliable source, instead of immediately calling them out — that almost always works better.

steps.title: Exercise
steps.body: Think of a short, friendly reply you'd give if someone in your group chat shared a fake message.
